This week's post is dedicated to my dad, who always has a watermelon-in-progress in his fridge, covered with an elastic shower cap.

Let’s be honest: this whole three-part series on the cucurbits family was aimed, all along, at that pinnacle summer experience, ye olde watermelon (Citrullus lanatus).1 Stepping back to view the family as a whole, we see a global story: whereas the Cucurbita genus originated in the Americas, and Cucumis in Asia (via Australia), Citrullus is a powerfully hydrating, botanically confusing gift from Africa. At first glance, “watermelon” is a wonderfully literal name compared to those evocatively figurative fruits, such as “honeydew” or “custard apple.” Indeed, the watermelon has such a high water content that it used to be carried on journeys like “a kind of nature-made canteen.” But that literalness conceals an apparent contradiction: wild and ancestral watermelons are xerophytic (“dry” + “plant”), requiring little water to grow. These sprawling annual vines first emerged in desert climates, from the Kordofan melons that grow in Sudan, and their deep taproots and durable leaves allow them to survive on almost nothing.

How melons do this is a small marvel to consider. A melon operates as a thermal buffer, maintaining internal temperatures significantly below the ambient air through a combination of structural insulation and cellular physics. Drawing moisture from the deep, cool soil, the vine drives cooling groundwater into the expanding “pepo”—the botanical term for this specialized berry—where it is held in a mesh of thin-walled cells. This massive internal volume, containing approximately 92% water, requires a large amount of thermal energy to change its temperature; in other words, it stays cool long into the heat of the day. Furthermore, the dense rind acts as a barrier against rising temperatures, while the plant's own leaf canopy shades it from the sun. These neat tricks allow the watermelon to function as a living thermal heatsink, resisting the peak fluctuations of the summer atmosphere to preserve a stable, cool environment for its developing seeds. No wonder the fruit was buried with pharaohs and painted on the walls of their tombs.

Obviously, watermelon is a pretty old fruit. Its intersection with human history falls roughly in a second generation between the oldest cultivated fruits—grapes, avocados, and especially figs—and modern newcomers such as strawberries, grapefruit, and kiwis. But the watermelon and its wild relatives were eaten first for their nutritious seeds, which have been recovered from 6,000-year-old archaeological sites in Libya. And while the flesh of those wild relatives is mostly bitter and often toxic, all parts of the watermelon’s fruit are now edible thanks to a genetic mutation that stopped its production of bitter cucurbitacins, while leaving them intact, as pest deterrents, in the rest of the plant. In addition to its succulent pulp and pickle-able rinds, which include many beneficial substances and properties, the historically significant seeds are again gaining culinary interest, especially in powder or flour form.

Botanically, the watermelon is considered a true pepo (a large berry with a hard rind and many seeds in a central pocket), not to be confused with soft-skinned true berries such as papaya and passionfruit. Unlike some thick-skinned pepos (think: pumpkin), you can eat it raw. In addition to the Kordofan melon from which it emerged, the watermelon shares a genus with six other species, with which it sometimes has been confused. The egusi melon (Citrullus mucosospermus), recently confirmed by molecular botanists as its own species, is now being studied for biotechnological applications, and its seeds (alongside those of the white-seed melon, Cucumeropsis mannii) remain an important part of West African cuisine. There are other sources of confusion, too: it was only in the past twenty years that scientists robustly distinguished the sweet red watermelon from several similar-looking relatives, including the toxic colocynth and the oldest member of Citrullus: the alien-looking and deceptively named Gemsbok cucumber.

The sweetness, the sustenance, the confusion, the weirdos—I guess the cucurbits are just another typical family, after all.

Welcome to the woodlands. There is, of course, more I would like to say about the late summer hærfest, but the call of the forest is irresistible, especially near the fall equinox, as the light slants through the trees and all that.

North American woodlands include more than 140 forest types, as recognized by the U.S. Forest Service. These are divided roughly between eastern and western formations, with coniferous softwood species dominating in the western portion of the continent and deciduous hardwood trees characterizing the eastern half. The “mighty oak,” as the English call it, is a keystone species across both of these halves and, indeed, the majority of the continent’s forests. It supports more life forms and provides more calories than most other trees: its nutritious acorns, up to 10,000 per tree in a mast year, support about 100 types of animals, and its abundant foliage sustains around 500 different types of caterpillars, which in turn are eaten by birds and small mammals. Oak forests also have played an important role in human diets from Europe to Asia, and especially as tended by indigenous Americans through burning and other practices. And they may yet play an important role in the future of food.

This is all in addition to the ink that oak galls provided for much of Euro-Mediterranean history, as I discussed in early June. And even before they facilitated Europe’s written culture, oak trees were often associated with both deities (or worshipped outright) and sacrificial killings—a fact Paul Laurence Dunbar transforms in his lynching poem, “The Haunted Oak”:

Pray why are you so bare, so bare, Oh, bough of the old oak-tree; And why, when I go through the shade you throw, Runs a shudder over me?

Whether scenery or sustenance, god or gallows, the oak reaches and tangles and expands, like the famous Angel Oak in South Carolina.

The northern red oak (Quercus rubra)—not to be confused with what is sometimes called the southern red oak (Quercus falcata)—is one of nearly 500 members of the Quercus genus (which includes an additional 150 to 200 natural hybrids). However, “red oaks” also correspond to a whole section of the Quercus genus, called Lobatae, which includes approximately 190 New World and high-latitude species (versus subsection Cerris, for Old World and mid-latitude species). Oaks are part of the beech family (Fagaceae), also home to beeches (obviously), chestnuts, and less common species, including chinquapins. They are trees of the northern hemisphere, originating in the Arctic (during a non-anthropogenically warm phase of the climate) and essential to the temperate landscapes and ecosystems across Asia, Europe, and North America. The northern red oak, in particular, is native to eastern North America and was called “red” by European settlers due to its fiery fall colors and pink-tinted wood—by contrast, the Ojibwe and Lenape call it wiisagi-mitigominzh and wisahkakw, respectively, due to the bitter, tannic taste of its acorns (prior to soaking or other processing). Red oaks can be distinguished by their jagged lobes and sharp, bristle tips; white oaks have rounded lobes but, perhaps surprisingly, also turn bright burgundy, orange, and other vibrant colors in the fall.

It’s still early fall here in New England; but in just a few weeks, we’ll all be seeing red.

Few trees in New England, except perhaps the marvelous paper birch (Betula papyrifera), have quite the visual appeal of the shagbark hickory. The distinction is in the name. A fully shagged-out trunk embodies something between an elegant cascade and a strewn-out mess—a poise we might all hope to achieve, if we are so lucky.

Hickory trees found their name in English by shortening the Algonquin or Powhatan word, pawcohiccora, which refers to the flour or milk made from crushing hickory nuts dry or in water. Their name thus embodies not only this culinary-cultural past but, as writers like Elspeth Hay (in her recent book, Feed Us With Trees) and food foresters around the country are demonstrating, a potential agricultural, social, and ecological future. After all, much of the North American continent, as well as regional and peasant cultures around the world, were once sustained by edible landscapes of fire-shaped forests that produced an abundance of nuts, other nourishing substances, and useful objects. Today, researchers and agroforesters across the Northeast and Midwest are making a healthy, delicious culinary oil from shagbark’s cousin, the Yellowbud, or bitternut, hickory (Carya cordiformis). This all made me curious about the forests that surround us here in New England.

Massachusetts, as the state likes to brag, is the third-densest state in the U.S. but also the 11th-most-forested. Thus, forests comprise a major variety of what are referred to politely, by the local government, as “the natural communities of Massachusetts”: these include formations such as “acidic rock cliff community” and “cultural grassland.” The hickory genus (Carya) contains 19 recognized species, 12 native to North American and seven to Southeast Asia). Hickories are close companions of oaks, including the northern red oak I wrote about last week. Whereas oaks are in the beech family (Fagaceae), hickories are in the walnut family (Juglandaceae); but both are grouped in the higher-level order of beeches (Fagales), all distinguished by the presence of a hard cupule (hull or husk) that partially or completely encloses their fruit.

Together, these two trees define the oak-hickory forest type that represents approximately one-third of the state’s forested land: that’s more than 1,000,000 acres! Such forests are home to some of my favorite plants, including witch-hazel and the pink lady’s slipper orchid. Oak-hickory forest is one of the more diverse types of oak communities, falling near the middle of a spectrum between dry, acidic scrub oak scrublands (where they mix with wild blueberries and other heath species) and riparian, flood-prone oak wetlands (where they mix with ash, willow, or sweetgum) Though companions, oaks and hickories do compete, with fast-growing oaks racing to the canopy while hickories root deep, establish a small stand, and wait in the under-canopy, perhaps for centuries, until an opening appears—a poise we might all hope to achieve, if we are so lucky.

Do you know a pawpaw fanatic? Venture more than a few minutes into conversation with someone interested in foraging or regional foodways, and you are likely to broach the subject. This custardy delectation, the largest native tree fruit in the U.S., has a curious backstory and is much beloved in such circles but otherwise hardly known. The reason is that the fruit is largely non-commercializable, because it spoils within days of picking. To find it, you’ll have more luck leaving behind the supermarket shelves and looking instead in the woods behind the store—at least for now (growers in Ohio, the heart of pawpaw territory, are experimenting with new techniques and strategies). Whether or not you love the fruit, which in my limited experience tastes like a cross between a banana and a mango, or a lightly cinnamoned pear, you are in for a surprise—a new constellation of flavors and sensations inviting you to find “a new language,” as Brillat-Savarin writes below, for your sapid experience.

Pawpaw (Asimina triloba) is a small deciduous tree or large shrub that can appear in the understory layer of forests across the eastern half of the U.S. Though its native range stops short of New England, planted trees have escaped here, and I've heard rumors of some good stands in (and tasted a few fruit from) Boston's outer suburbs. The tree grows big leaves, up to a foot long, and can reproduce via root suckers that emerge from underground as clones of the parent tree. It also produces hermaphroditic flowers, containing both stamens and carpels, that smell slightly rotten or yeasty—the tree’s ploy to attract the flies and beetles that it needs to bring pollen from other plants.

Pawpaw is a member of the soursop or “custard apple” family (Annonaceae), and the only one native to temperate latitudes. Its fruit is what some scientists consider a “neotropical anachronism”: it may have been food for the gomphotheres, a long-extinct relative of the elephants that once wandered the North American landmass. In the current day, pawpaws are closely associated with a striking butterfly, the zebra swallowtail (Protographium marcellus, formerly Eurytides marcellus), whose caterpillars feed exclusively on pawpaw foliage. Their relationship parallels that of monarch and milkweed, except that the zebra swallowtail is not involved in pollinating the pawpaw. Instead, it is in an obligate relationship, as the butterfly gains nourishment and a defense mechanism (through the pawpaw’s toxic acetogenins—concentrated in the leaves, bark, and seeds) in exchange for nothing but looking so beautiful. This dependency means that the butterflies are rarely found more than a few hundred yards (up to a mile) from their host patch of pawpaws; if you see one, you are probably also in the company of a special tree.

Is it a bush? Is it a tree? Is it a poison? Is it lemonade? In the lower gaps of the forest, or in its damaged peripheries, the sumac thrives. Like the pawpaw, it often spreads through root suckers, producing a grove of clones in meadow edges, riverbanks, or cleared land. Its conical flowers and then spike-like berry clusters develop over the summer, and its leaves erupt into vibrant colors in the early fall. The plant’s leaves and bark contain tannins that were used for centuries, around the world, to tan light and flexible leathers and as a mordant to dye fabrics. In North America, the berries were steeped to produce a brilliant pink, slightly acidic tea comparable to lemonade. And after falling out of favor in European cuisines, the tart, peppery flavor profile persisted in the Middle East and is now poised for a global comeback.

The sumac genus (Rhus) contains somewhere between 35 and 100+ species, depending on who’s counting—47 is an officially recognized number—with roughly 20 species native to North America. Sumac plants can be found in temperate regions around the globe, although the genus may have originated in western North America (the oldest known fossils come from Washington State). The sumac genus lends its common name to the broader sumac family (Anacardiaceae), perhaps more commonly known as the cashew family, which contains approximately 80 genera and 850+ species, including those that grow mangos, cashews, pistachios, and marulas. So-called poison sumac (Toxicodendron vernix), which I for some reason vaguely feared as a child, is in a separate genus within that larger family, along with poisons oak and ivy. These species all produce the highly inflammatory resin, urushiol, known for occasionally causing “mango mouth” and for harming the people—many of them women, children, and forced laborers—who process cashews. But of course, because botany makes so much sense, the true sumacs for which the plant family is known do not produce urushiol.

Both the common and Latin names have interesting etymologies. The descriptor “staghorn” is mostly transparent. It was adopted by English settlers in North America to distinguish the plant’s fuzzy, forking branches from its smoother brethren, such as the aptly named smooth sumac (Rhus glabra). This association with horns was formalized in the 1750s, when Carl Linnaeus and his student, Ericus Torner, identified the plant as Ramis hirtis uti typhi cervini (“with branches hairy like antlers in velvet"). The word “sumac” has an even longer history, descending from Arabic (summaq) and Classical Syriac/Aramaic (summāqā) words for “dark red,” which were absorbed into Medieval Latin and Old French around the 13th century. Though the word first referred specifically to the chopped berries of the plants, its meaning later expanded to include other parts of the plant used for tanning leather, dyeing textiles, or as a medicinal astringent. Finally, by the mid-1540s, it was applied to the living plants themselves.

As for the Latin, the name of the “Rhus” genus comes from the classical Latin and Greek names for sumac plants, notably Sicilian or tanner’s sumac (Rhus coriaria), known for its leather-tanning and dyeing properties. The typhina descriptor for staghorn sumac also was supplied by Linnaeus and Torner, in their comparison of the plant to the hairy antlers of a male deer (typhi cervini)—although, that description itself may itself echo the cattail (typha), another plant named for its fuzzy spike. Some might see this as a muddle of language and taxonomy. But that muddle embodies the fuzzy perceptions and tangled analogies that have built our basic picture of the world around us.

I felt nearly obligated, given the time of year, to dedicate this week’s entry to the venerable pumpkin, that special gourd so eternally loved and multifariously depicted by Yayoi Kusama (may she rest in peace). But in the spirit of veering, I present instead a more mysterious offering: a non-photosynthesizing parasite nonetheless described by Emily Dickinson as “the preferred flower of life.”

Enter the ghost pipe (Monotropa uniflora), also called by many other tantalizing names: ghost flower, Indian pipe, Dutchman’s pipe, American iceplant, corpse plant (not to be confused with the iconic corpse flower), convulsion root/weed, death plant, eyebright, fitroot, and—cherry on top—fairy smoke. The plant’s Latin binomial is literal but beautiful, meaning roughly a “single-turning” (monos + tropos) “one-flower” (unus + flos); although the OED reaches back even further, as Arnold Zwicky notes, deriving Monotropa from an ancient Greek word that means “living alone, solitary.” These descriptions are all apt. The ghost pipe’s head-bowing blooms—compared by another nineteenth-century poet to nuns—grow throughout the summer, in dark, moist patches of the forest, near the trunks of the trees that feed and shade them. By autumn, however, the plant has turned from ghost to zombie, as its nodding head lifts to release its seeds, and the now-erect stalk dries into blacks and browns.

Ghost pipes are considered native across many regions of North America, as well as high-altitude regions of Central and South America, and throughout Eastern Asia. They are part of the monotropes subfamily (Monotropoideae), comprising approximately 15 to 20 species within the heath or heather family (Ericaceae), which also includes cranberries, blueberries, and the various rhododendrons. The ghostly monotropes are notable as non-photosynthesizing plants, surviving mysteriously without chlorophyll (hence their lack of green) and in extremely simplified form, often as single inflorescences rather than complex shrubs or trees. How does this phantom survive in the dark? As Merlin Sheldrake explains below, it took botanists more than a hundred years of speculation and debate until the facts became clear; over a series a discoveries that drastically changed our understanding of plants, fungi, and life on earth generally, they described the process of myco-heterotrophy that allows the monotropes to extract sustenance indirectly, not through a tree itself but from the fungi that symbiotically surrounds its roots.

Mirroring its natural environment, this species has survived in a special niche of modern poetry. Dickinson wrote her riddle-like poem about the ghost pipe, or Indian pipe (included below), around 1879; her correspondent and posthumous editor, Mabel Loomis Todd, titled it “The Spirit” when she published it in 1896. The plant appeared in other nineteenth century poems by Catharine Esther Beecher (sister of Harriet Beecher Stowe) and Mary Potter Thacher Higginson; and later in haunting works by Sylvia Plath, G.C. Waldrep, and Christine Butterworth-McDermott. Together, these works offer a quiet, fragile, surprising recurrence—flowering once but surviving underground in roots that survive the winter.
